## Cognitive Science / Personal Knowledge Management

> [!further-exploration] From: [[pkm-working-memory-cognitive-offloading-foundational-report-2026-04-05|pkm-working-memory-cognitive-offloading-foundational-report-2026-04-05]]
> > [!topic-idea] **[[Spaced-Repetition-Systems]]** — Deep Implementation Architecture
> > **Description:** While this report establishes the cognitive science justification for spaced repetition in PKM, a dedicated Practitioner's Field Guide treating SR implementation in depth — algorithm types (SM-2, FSRS), card design principles for different knowledge types (conceptual, procedural, cloze), integration with Obsidian workflows, optimal daily review volumes, and failure mode analysis — would serve as a high-value companion resource.
> > **Connection to this report:** Section 6 identifies SRS as a high-leverage implementation of offloading-optimised review; Section 8.8 seeds provide starting material. The full cognitive case (spacing effect, testing effect, generation effect) is summarised but not operationalised for implementation.
> > **Priority:** Critical
> > **Suggested Report Type:** Practitioner's Field Guide
> > **Prerequisites:** [[Spaced-Repetition]], [[Desirable-Difficulties]], [[Long-Term-Memory]]
> 
> > [!topic-idea] **[[Distributed-Cognition]]** — Foundational Theory and Applications
> > **Description:** This report uses Hutchins' distributed cognition framework as context but does not treat it foundationally. A Foundational Report on distributed cognition would cover the theoretical framework in full (Hutchins 1995, Salomon 1993), its relationship to the extended mind debate, empirical studies of distributed systems (ship navigation, air traffic control, surgical teams), and implications for organisational knowledge management and multi-person collaborative PKM.
> > **Connection to this report:** Distributed cognition provides the systems-level empirical grounding that the philosophical extended mind thesis lacks; it also opens the question of how PKM principles extend to collaborative or multi-person knowledge management contexts, which this report treats only in the Far Transfer section.
> > **Priority:** High
> > **Suggested Report Type:** Foundational Report
> > **Prerequisites:** [[Extended-Mind-Thesis]], [[Cognitive-Offloading]], [[Embodied-Cognition]]
> 
> > [!topic-idea] **[[Desirable-Difficulties]]** — Learning Science and PKM Application
> > **Description:** The Bjork desirable difficulties framework (spacing, interleaving, testing, generation, contextual interference) has direct design implications for PKM that this report treats only tangentially. A Foundational Report on desirable difficulties would establish the empirical evidence base for each difficulty type, explain the mechanistic account (encoding specificity, retrieval practice effects, contextual reinstatement), and develop design principles for building desirable difficulties into PKM review workflows without adding extraneous load.
> > **Connection to this report:** The Generative Investment Principle and the Scaffold-Dependence Risk discussion both invoke desirable difficulties logic. The full framework would provide the empirical foundation for the normative claims made in these sections.
> > **Priority:** High
> > **Suggested Report Type:** Foundational Report
> > **Prerequisites:** [[Long-Term-Memory]], [[Spaced-Repetition]], [[Generative-Processing]]
> 
> > [!topic-idea] **[[Metacognition]]** — Self-Regulated Learning and PKM
> > **Description:** A significant gap in the current report is the metacognitive dimension: how do practitioners monitor the quality of their offloading, detect when the substitution trap is operating, evaluate whether their PKB is functioning as genuine extended cognition or merely as an archive, and regulate their processing strategies accordingly? A Foundational Report on metacognition in the context of [[Self-Regulated-Learning]] would address: metacognitive monitoring of learning, calibration research, the Dunning-Kruger dynamic in PKM, and specific metacognitive practices for PKM quality assurance.
> > **Connection to this report:** Section 6 identifies the distinction between replacement and augmentation uses of PKM as a metacognitive challenge that practitioners handle poorly. The entire framework implies metacognitive demands without explicitly building them out.
> > **Priority:** High
> > **Suggested Report Type:** Foundational Report
> > **Prerequisites:** [[Metacognition]], [[Self-Regulated-Learning]], [[Cognitive-Monitoring]]
> 
> > [!topic-idea] **[[PKB-Architecture]]** — Systems Design for Extended Cognition
> > **Description:** This report establishes the cognitive principles that constrain effective PKB design but does not develop a comprehensive systems architecture. A Comparative Architecture Report comparing major PKM architectures (Zettelkasten, PARA, Johnny Decimal, LYT, PPV) evaluated against the seven design principles developed here would provide practitioners with an evidence-grounded framework for making architecture choices. The evaluative criteria established in this report — Trust Condition satisfaction, Semantic Density, Retrieval-as-Computation capability, Extraneous Load profile — are directly applicable as evaluation dimensions.
> > **Connection to this report:** The design principles in Section 5 constitute implicit evaluation criteria for any PKB architecture. Making that evaluation explicit would bridge the gap between theoretical framework and architecture selection.
> > **Priority:** Critical
> > **Suggested Report Type:** Comparative Architecture
> > **Prerequisites:** [[Personal-Knowledge-Management]], [[Obsidian-PKB-Architecture]], [[Zettelkasten]], [[PARA-Method]]

> [!further-exploration] From: [[schema-externalization-pkb-long-term-memory-foundational-report-2026-04-05|schema-externalization-pkb-long-term-memory-foundational-report-2026-04-05]]
> 

> [!topic-idea] From: [[schema-externalization-pkb-long-term-memory-foundational-report-2026-04-05|schema-externalization-pkb-long-term-memory-foundational-report-2026-04-05]]
> **The Empirical Testing of the Bidirectional Enrichment Hypothesis**
> 
> **Description:** Design longitudinal studies measuring internal schema development in PKB practitioners as a function of PKB schema-fidelity. This would require validated measures of both PKB schema-fidelity and internal schema organization (concept mapping, clinical interview, knowledge structure assessment batteries). The hypothesis generates specific testable predictions that could be investigated with existing methods in educational and cognitive psychology.
> **Connection to this report:** The Bidirectional Enrichment Hypothesis is the central original contribution of this report; it is well-motivated but untested. Empirical investigation would either validate and flesh out the mechanism or identify where the synthesis breaks down.
> **Priority:** Critical
> **Suggested report type:** Practitioner's Field Guide
> **Prerequisites:** [[Schema-Theory]], [[Research-Methods-in-Cognitive-Psychology]], [[Cognitive-Assessment]]

> [!topic-idea] From: [[schema-externalization-pkb-long-term-memory-foundational-report-2026-04-05|schema-externalization-pkb-long-term-memory-foundational-report-2026-04-05]]
> **The Cognitive Science of Note-Taking and Knowledge Construction**
> 
> **Description:** A systematic review of the experimental literature on note-taking, note retrieval, and the conditions under which externalized notes support vs. replace internal knowledge construction. This would synthesize research from Mueller & Oppenheimer (2014) on laptop vs. longhand notes, Karpicke's retrieval-augmented note-taking studies, and the emerging PKM research literature.
> **Connection to this report:** Section 3 and Section 7 draw on this research; a dedicated treatment would provide depth on the specific conditions under which externalization supports vs. undermines schema formation.
> **Priority:** High
> **Suggested report type:** Foundational Report
> **Prerequisites:** [[Memory-Systems]], [[Learning-Science]], [[Cognitive-Load-Theory]]

> [!topic-idea] From: [[schema-externalization-pkb-long-term-memory-foundational-report-2026-04-05|schema-externalization-pkb-long-term-memory-foundational-report-2026-04-05]]
> **Schema Externalization Across Knowledge Modalities: Visual, Verbal, Mathematical**
> 
> **Description:** Different knowledge domains organize schemas differently — mathematical schemas are highly symbolic and procedural; verbal/conceptual schemas are propositional and analogical; visuospatial schemas involve mental rotation and topological relationships. How does schema externalization interact with these modality differences? Should PKB design differ by domain?
> **Connection to this report:** This report focuses on conceptual/verbal schema externalization (the dominant mode in text-based PKBs). The modality question is acknowledged but not addressed in depth.
> **Priority:** High
> **Suggested report type:** Comparative Architecture
> **Prerequisites:** [[Long-Term-Memory]], [[Dual-Coding-Theory]], [[Spatial-Cognition]], [[Mathematical-Cognition]]

> [!topic-idea] From: [[schema-externalization-pkb-long-term-memory-foundational-report-2026-04-05|schema-externalization-pkb-long-term-memory-foundational-report-2026-04-05]]
> **Transactive Memory Systems in Teams and the Collective Schema Externalization Problem**
> 
> **Description:** When multiple practitioners share a PKB or build linked knowledge systems, schema externalization becomes a collective coordination problem. The group's transactive memory system (who knows what, who knows who knows what) must be externalized in a way that mirrors collective rather than individual schemas. What principles govern this?
> **Connection to this report:** Section 5 briefly notes distributed cognition contexts. Team-level or community-level PKBs represent a significant practical frontier where this report's individual-level framework needs extension.
> **Priority:** High
> **Suggested report type:** Foundational Report
> **Prerequisites:** [[Transactive-Memory-Systems]], [[Distributed-Cognition]], [[Collaborative-Learning]], [[Knowledge-Management]]

> [!topic-idea] From: [[schema-externalization-pkb-long-term-memory-foundational-report-2026-04-05|schema-externalization-pkb-long-term-memory-foundational-report-2026-04-05]]
> **Historical and Cultural Variability in External Schema-Like Structures**
> 
> **Description:** Oral cultures, manuscript traditions, codex cultures, and digital cultures have each developed external schema structures — memory palaces, commonplace books, card indices, wiki graphs. A historical-genealogical examination would reveal what schema externalization problems each era faced, what structural solutions emerged, and what we can learn from the intellectual history of externalizing schema-like structure.
> **Connection to this report:** The cognitive science framework presented here illuminates what these historical practices were doing cognitively, and the historical survey would reveal practical wisdom the cognitive science framework might miss.
> **Priority:** Medium
> **Suggested report type:** Historical-Genealogical Report
> **Prerequisites:** [[Memory-Palace]], [[Commonplace-Books]], [[Zettelkasten-Method]], [[History-of-Knowledge-Management]]

> [!further-exploration] From: [[pkm-working-memory-cognitive-offloading-foundational-report-2026-04-05|pkm-working-memory-cognitive-offloading-foundational-report-2026-04-05]]

> > **Connection to this report:** The design principles in Section 5 constitute implicit evaluation criteria for any PKB architecture. Making that evaluation explicit would bridge the gap between theoretical framework and architecture selection.
> > **Priority:** Critical
> > **Suggested Report Type:** Comparative Architecture
> > **Prerequisites:** [[Personal-Knowledge-Management]], [[Obsidian-PKB-Architecture]], [[Zettelkasten]], [[PARA-Method]]

> [!further-exploration] From: [[schema-externalization-pkb-long-term-memory-foundational-report-2026-04-05|schema-externalization-pkb-long-term-memory-foundational-report-2026-04-05]]
> 

> [!topic-idea] From: [[schema-externalization-pkb-long-term-memory-foundational-report-2026-04-05|schema-externalization-pkb-long-term-memory-foundational-report-2026-04-05]]
> **The Empirical Testing of the Bidirectional Enrichment Hypothesis**
> 
> **Description:** Design longitudinal studies measuring internal schema development in PKB practitioners as a function of PKB schema-fidelity. This would require validated measures of both PKB schema-fidelity and internal schema organization (concept mapping, clinical interview, knowledge structure assessment batteries). The hypothesis generates specific testable predictions that could be investigated with existing methods in educational and cognitive psychology.
> **Connection to this report:** The Bidirectional Enrichment Hypothesis is the central original contribution of this report; it is well-motivated but untested. Empirical investigation would either validate and flesh out the mechanism or identify where the synthesis breaks down.
> **Priority:** Critical
> **Suggested report type:** Practitioner's Field Guide
> **Prerequisites:** [[Schema-Theory]], [[Research-Methods-in-Cognitive-Psychology]], [[Cognitive-Assessment]]

> [!topic-idea] From: [[schema-externalization-pkb-long-term-memory-foundational-report-2026-04-05|schema-externalization-pkb-long-term-memory-foundational-report-2026-04-05]]
> **The Cognitive Science of Note-Taking and Knowledge Construction**
> 
> **Description:** A systematic review of the experimental literature on note-taking, note retrieval, and the conditions under which externalized notes support vs. replace internal knowledge construction. This would synthesize research from Mueller & Oppenheimer (2014) on laptop vs. longhand notes, Karpicke's retrieval-augmented note-taking studies, and the emerging PKM research literature.
> **Connection to this report:** Section 3 and Section 7 draw on this research; a dedicated treatment would provide depth on the specific conditions under which externalization supports vs. undermines schema formation.
> **Priority:** High
> **Suggested report type:** Foundational Report
> **Prerequisites:** [[Memory-Systems]], [[Learning-Science]], [[Cognitive-Load-Theory]]

> [!topic-idea] From: [[schema-externalization-pkb-long-term-memory-foundational-report-2026-04-05|schema-externalization-pkb-long-term-memory-foundational-report-2026-04-05]]
> **Schema Externalization Across Knowledge Modalities: Visual, Verbal, Mathematical**
> 
> **Description:** Different knowledge domains organize schemas differently — mathematical schemas are highly symbolic and procedural; verbal/conceptual schemas are propositional and analogical; visuospatial schemas involve mental rotation and topological relationships. How does schema externalization interact with these modality differences? Should PKB design differ by domain?
> **Connection to this report:** This report focuses on conceptual/verbal schema externalization (the dominant mode in text-based PKBs). The modality question is acknowledged but not addressed in depth.
> **Priority:** High
> **Suggested report type:** Comparative Architecture
> **Prerequisites:** [[Long-Term-Memory]], [[Dual-Coding-Theory]], [[Spatial-Cognition]], [[Mathematical-Cognition]]

> [!topic-idea] From: [[schema-externalization-pkb-long-term-memory-foundational-report-2026-04-05|schema-externalization-pkb-long-term-memory-foundational-report-2026-04-05]]
> **Transactive Memory Systems in Teams and the Collective Schema Externalization Problem**
> 
> **Description:** When multiple practitioners share a PKB or build linked knowledge systems, schema externalization becomes a collective coordination problem. The group's transactive memory system (who knows what, who knows who knows what) must be externalized in a way that mirrors collective rather than individual schemas. What principles govern this?
> **Connection to this report:** Section 5 briefly notes distributed cognition contexts. Team-level or community-level PKBs represent a significant practical frontier where this report's individual-level framework needs extension.
> **Priority:** High
> **Suggested report type:** Foundational Report
> **Prerequisites:** [[Transactive-Memory-Systems]], [[Distributed-Cognition]], [[Collaborative-Learning]], [[Knowledge-Management]]

> [!topic-idea] From: [[schema-externalization-pkb-long-term-memory-foundational-report-2026-04-05|schema-externalization-pkb-long-term-memory-foundational-report-2026-04-05]]
> **Historical and Cultural Variability in External Schema-Like Structures**
> 
> **Description:** Oral cultures, manuscript traditions, codex cultures, and digital cultures have each developed external schema structures — memory palaces, commonplace books, card indices, wiki graphs. A historical-genealogical examination would reveal what schema externalization problems each era faced, what structural solutions emerged, and what we can learn from the intellectual history of externalizing schema-like structure.
> **Connection to this report:** The cognitive science framework presented here illuminates what these historical practices were doing cognitively, and the historical survey would reveal practical wisdom the cognitive science framework might miss.
> **Priority:** Medium
> **Suggested report type:** Historical-Genealogical Report
> **Prerequisites:** [[Memory-Palace]], [[Commonplace-Books]], [[Zettelkasten-Method]], [[History-of-Knowledge-Management]]

> [!further-exploration] From: [[pkm-working-memory-cognitive-offloading-foundational-report-2026-04-05|pkm-working-memory-cognitive-offloading-foundational-report-2026-04-05]]
> > [!topic-idea] **[[Spaced-Repetition-Systems]]** — Deep Implementation Architecture
> > **Description:** While this report establishes the cognitive science justification for spaced repetition in PKM, a dedicated Practitioner's Field Guide treating SR implementation in depth — algorithm types (SM-2, FSRS), card design principles for different knowledge types (conceptual, procedural, cloze), integration with Obsidian workflows, optimal daily review volumes, and failure mode analysis — would serve as a high-value companion resource.
> > **Connection to this report:** Section 6 identifies SRS as a high-leverage implementation of offloading-optimised review; Section 8.8 seeds provide starting material. The full cognitive case (spacing effect, testing effect, generation effect) is summarised but not operationalised for implementation.
> > **Priority:** Critical
> > **Suggested Report Type:** Practitioner's Field Guide
> > **Prerequisites:** [[Spaced-Repetition]], [[Desirable-Difficulties]], [[Long-Term-Memory]]
> 
> > [!topic-idea] **[[Distributed-Cognition]]** — Foundational Theory and Applications
> > **Description:** This report uses Hutchins' distributed cognition framework as context but does not treat it foundationally. A Foundational Report on distributed cognition would cover the theoretical framework in full (Hutchins 1995, Salomon 1993), its relationship to the extended mind debate, empirical studies of distributed systems (ship navigation, air traffic control, surgical teams), and implications for organisational knowledge management and multi-person collaborative PKM.
> > **Connection to this report:** Distributed cognition provides the systems-level empirical grounding that the philosophical extended mind thesis lacks; it also opens the question of how PKM principles extend to collaborative or multi-person knowledge management contexts, which this report treats only in the Far Transfer section.
> > **Priority:** High
> > **Suggested Report Type:** Foundational Report
> > **Prerequisites:** [[Extended-Mind-Thesis]], [[Cognitive-Offloading]], [[Embodied-Cognition]]
> 
> > [!topic-idea] **[[Desirable-Difficulties]]** — Learning Science and PKM Application
> > **Description:** The Bjork desirable difficulties framework (spacing, interleaving, testing, generation, contextual interference) has direct design implications for PKM that this report treats only tangentially. A Foundational Report on desirable difficulties would establish the empirical evidence base for each difficulty type, explain the mechanistic account (encoding specificity, retrieval practice effects, contextual reinstatement), and develop design principles for building desirable difficulties into PKM review workflows without adding extraneous load.
> > **Connection to this report:** The Generative Investment Principle and the Scaffold-Dependence Risk discussion both invoke desirable difficulties logic. The full framework would provide the empirical foundation for the normative claims made in these sections.
> > **Priority:** High
> > **Suggested Report Type:** Foundational Report
> > **Prerequisites:** [[Long-Term-Memory]], [[Spaced-Repetition]], [[Generative-Processing]]
> 
> > [!topic-idea] **[[Metacognition]]** — Self-Regulated Learning and PKM
> > **Description:** A significant gap in the current report is the metacognitive dimension: how do practitioners monitor the quality of their offloading, detect when the substitution trap is operating, evaluate whether their PKB is functioning as genuine extended cognition or merely as an archive, and regulate their processing strategies accordingly? A Foundational Report on metacognition in the context of [[Self-Regulated-Learning]] would address: metacognitive monitoring of learning, calibration research, the Dunning-Kruger dynamic in PKM, and specific metacognitive practices for PKM quality assurance.
> > **Connection to this report:** Section 6 identifies the distinction between replacement and augmentation uses of PKM as a metacognitive challenge that practitioners handle poorly. The entire framework implies metacognitive demands without explicitly building them out.
> > **Priority:** High
> > **Suggested Report Type:** Foundational Report
> > **Prerequisites:** [[Metacognition]], [[Self-Regulated-Learning]], [[Cognitive-Monitoring]]
> 
> > [!topic-idea] **[[PKB-Architecture]]** — Systems Design for Extended Cognition
> > **Description:** This report establishes the cognitive principles that constrain effective PKB design but does not develop a comprehensive systems architecture. A Comparative Architecture Report comparing major PKM architectures (Zettelkasten, PARA, Johnny Decimal, LYT, PPV) evaluated against the seven design principles developed here would provide practitioners with an evidence-grounded framework for making architecture choices. The evaluative criteria established in this report — Trust Condition satisfaction, Semantic Density, Retrieval-as-Computation capability, Extraneous Load profile — are directly applicable as evaluation dimensions.
> > **Connection to this report:** The design principles in Section 5 constitute implicit evaluation criteria for any PKB architecture. Making that evaluation explicit would bridge the gap between theoretical framework and architecture selection.
> > **Priority:** Critical
> > **Suggested Report Type:** Comparative Architecture
> > **Prerequisites:** [[Personal-Knowledge-Management]], [[Obsidian-PKB-Architecture]], [[Zettelkasten]], [[PARA-Method]]

## Cognitive Science / Reading Comprehension

> [!further-exploration] From: [[developing-reading-comprehension-academic-texts-foundational-report-2026-04-08|developing-reading-comprehension-academic-texts-foundational-report-2026-04-08]]
> 

> [!topic-idea] From: [[developing-reading-comprehension-academic-texts-foundational-report-2026-04-08|developing-reading-comprehension-academic-texts-foundational-report-2026-04-08]]
> **[[Disciplinary-Literacy-and-Reading-Across-the-Curriculum]]**
> 
> **Description:** Disciplinary literacy research investigates how reading practices, inference types, and comprehension standards differ systematically across academic disciplines — what it means to read like a historian, scientist, mathematician, or literary critic. This report establishes that inference generation is partially domain-specific; a dedicated disciplinary literacy note would elaborately map these differences and their instructional implications.
> 
> **Connection to this report:** Section 5's finding that disciplinary inference generation requires disciplinary schemas creates a direct rationale for investigating what reading "looks like" across specific disciplines.
> 
> **Priority:** High
> 
> **Suggested report type:** Comparative Architecture — comparing reading practices and epistemic standards across 4–5 major academic disciplines.
> 
> **Prerequisites:** [[Situation-Model]], [[Schema-Theory]], [[Walter-Kintsch]]

> [!topic-idea] From: [[developing-reading-comprehension-academic-texts-foundational-report-2026-04-08|developing-reading-comprehension-academic-texts-foundational-report-2026-04-08]]
> **[[Second-Language-Academic-Reading-Comprehension]]**
> 
> **Description:** Academic reading comprehension in a second language introduces additional layers of complexity — L2 vocabulary gaps, cross-linguistic schema conflicts, syntactic parsing overhead, and the interplay of L1 schemas with L2 text structures. This is a substantial independent research tradition with its own theoretical models (e.g., the Linguistic Threshold Hypothesis, Cummins' Common Underlying Proficiency) and instructional implications for the rapidly growing population of English-as-an-additional-language academic readers.
> 
> **Connection to this report:** The vocabulary coverage threshold finding (98%) is even more pressing for L2 readers; the schema interference problem has a cross-linguistic dimension; the Matthew Effect operates within and across languages.
> 
> **Priority:** High
> 
> **Suggested report type:** Foundational Report — a comprehensive treatment of L2 academic reading comprehension as a field.
> 
> **Prerequisites:** [[Vocabulary-Acquisition-for-Reading-Automaticity]], [[Schema-Theory]], [[Verbal-Efficiency-Theory]]

> [!topic-idea] From: [[developing-reading-comprehension-academic-texts-foundational-report-2026-04-08|developing-reading-comprehension-academic-texts-foundational-report-2026-04-08]]
> **[[Reciprocal-Teaching-Research-Base-and-Implementation-Evidence]]**
> 
> **Description:** A focused critical analysis of the reciprocal teaching research literature — including the original Palincsar & Brown (1984) studies, the meta-analyses, the implementation challenges at scale, and the modifications proposed for secondary and tertiary contexts. This report treated reciprocal teaching as an intervention with a positive evidence base; a focused critical analysis would interrogate that evidence more rigorously.
> 
> **Connection to this report:** Reciprocal Teaching is the primary intervention recommendation in Section 7; a deeper evidence review would strengthen or qualify this claim.
> 
> **Priority:** Medium
> 
> **Suggested report type:** Annotated Critical Analysis — with Claude's reasoning about evidence quality made explicit.
> 
> **Prerequisites:** [[Comprehension-Monitoring]], [[Metacognition]], [[Ann-Brown]]

> [!topic-idea] From: [[developing-reading-comprehension-academic-texts-foundational-report-2026-04-08|developing-reading-comprehension-academic-texts-foundational-report-2026-04-08]]
> **[[Vocabulary-Acquisition-and-Reading-Development-Longitudinal-Research]]**
> 
> **Description:** Longitudinal studies tracking vocabulary development and reading comprehension from early schooling through secondary and tertiary education provide the empirical evidence base for the Matthew Effect and for vocabulary instruction priorities. A dedicated note synthesising the major longitudinal datasets (Hart & Risley, NICHD Early Child Care Research Network, the Rotterdam studies) would provide the developmental evidence grounding that this report's cross-sectional synthesis cannot supply.
> 
> **Connection to this report:** The Matthew Effect claim (Section 2, Section 7) is based on cross-sectional and short-term longitudinal evidence; the developmental trajectory claim needs long-term longitudinal evidence to stand on its strongest footing.
> 
> **Priority:** Medium
> 
> **Suggested report type:** Historical-Genealogical Report — tracing the development of vocabulary and reading research from Hart & Risley (1995) through the 30-million word gap debate through contemporary precision.
> 
> **Prerequisites:** [[Matthew-Effect-in-Reading]], [[Vocabulary-Acquisition-for-Reading-Automaticity]], [[Reading-Fluency]]

> [!topic-idea] From: [[developing-reading-comprehension-academic-texts-foundational-report-2026-04-08|developing-reading-comprehension-academic-texts-foundational-report-2026-04-08]]
> **[[Cognitive-Load-Theory-and-Academic-Text-Design]]**
> 
> **Description:** If academic reading comprehension is constrained by working memory capacity and processing efficiency, then academic text *design* — how authors structure, signpost, and format texts — directly shapes the reading comprehension demands placed on readers. Applying Sweller's Cognitive Load Theory to academic text design would yield evidence-based principles for authors, editors, and instructors who produce academic materials for readers at different expertise levels.
> 
> **Connection to this report:** The working memory load-sharing account from Section 2 (Verbal Efficiency Theory) and the CI model's implicit working memory demands create a direct logical connection to text design principles.
> 
> **Priority:** Exploratory
> 
> **Suggested report type:** Practitioner's Field Guide — with practical protocols for academic text authors and instructional material designers.
> 
> **Prerequisites:** [[Cognitive-Load-Theory]], [[cognitive-load-theory-foundational-report-2026-03-11]], [[Working-Memory-in-Reading]]

> [!further-exploration] From: [[developing-reading-comprehension-academic-texts-foundational-report-2026-04-08|developing-reading-comprehension-academic-texts-foundational-report-2026-04-08]]

> **Prerequisites:** [[Vocabulary-Acquisition-for-Reading-Automaticity]], [[Schema-Theory]], [[Verbal-Efficiency-Theory]]

> [!topic-idea] From: [[developing-reading-comprehension-academic-texts-foundational-report-2026-04-08|developing-reading-comprehension-academic-texts-foundational-report-2026-04-08]]
> **[[Reciprocal-Teaching-Research-Base-and-Implementation-Evidence]]**
> 
> **Description:** A focused critical analysis of the reciprocal teaching research literature — including the original Palincsar & Brown (1984) studies, the meta-analyses, the implementation challenges at scale, and the modifications proposed for secondary and tertiary contexts. This report treated reciprocal teaching as an intervention with a positive evidence base; a focused critical analysis would interrogate that evidence more rigorously.
> 
> **Connection to this report:** Reciprocal Teaching is the primary intervention recommendation in Section 7; a deeper evidence review would strengthen or qualify this claim.
> 
> **Priority:** Medium
> 
> **Suggested report type:** Annotated Critical Analysis — with Claude's reasoning about evidence quality made explicit.
> 
> **Prerequisites:** [[Comprehension-Monitoring]], [[Metacognition]], [[Ann-Brown]]

> [!topic-idea] From: [[developing-reading-comprehension-academic-texts-foundational-report-2026-04-08|developing-reading-comprehension-academic-texts-foundational-report-2026-04-08]]
> **[[Vocabulary-Acquisition-and-Reading-Development-Longitudinal-Research]]**
> 
> **Description:** Longitudinal studies tracking vocabulary development and reading comprehension from early schooling through secondary and tertiary education provide the empirical evidence base for the Matthew Effect and for vocabulary instruction priorities. A dedicated note synthesising the major longitudinal datasets (Hart & Risley, NICHD Early Child Care Research Network, the Rotterdam studies) would provide the developmental evidence grounding that this report's cross-sectional synthesis cannot supply.
> 
> **Connection to this report:** The Matthew Effect claim (Section 2, Section 7) is based on cross-sectional and short-term longitudinal evidence; the developmental trajectory claim needs long-term longitudinal evidence to stand on its strongest footing.
> 
> **Priority:** Medium
> 
> **Suggested report type:** Historical-Genealogical Report — tracing the development of vocabulary and reading research from Hart & Risley (1995) through the 30-million word gap debate through contemporary precision.
> 
> **Prerequisites:** [[Matthew-Effect-in-Reading]], [[Vocabulary-Acquisition-for-Reading-Automaticity]], [[Reading-Fluency]]

> [!topic-idea] From: [[developing-reading-comprehension-academic-texts-foundational-report-2026-04-08|developing-reading-comprehension-academic-texts-foundational-report-2026-04-08]]
> **[[Cognitive-Load-Theory-and-Academic-Text-Design]]**
> 
> **Description:** If academic reading comprehension is constrained by working memory capacity and processing efficiency, then academic text *design* — how authors structure, signpost, and format texts — directly shapes the reading comprehension demands placed on readers. Applying Sweller's Cognitive Load Theory to academic text design would yield evidence-based principles for authors, editors, and instructors who produce academic materials for readers at different expertise levels.
> 
> **Connection to this report:** The working memory load-sharing account from Section 2 (Verbal Efficiency Theory) and the CI model's implicit working memory demands create a direct logical connection to text design principles.
> 
> **Priority:** Exploratory
> 
> **Suggested report type:** Practitioner's Field Guide — with practical protocols for academic text authors and instructional material designers.
> 
> **Prerequisites:** [[Cognitive-Load-Theory]], [[cognitive-load-theory-foundational-report-2026-03-11]], [[Working-Memory-in-Reading]]

## Cognitive Psychology

> [!further-exploration] From: [[metacognition-silent-reading-focused-analysis-2026-03-21|metacognition-silent-reading-focused-analysis-2026-03-21]]
> **Deepening Your Practice**
> 
> > [!topic-idea] [[Metacognitive-Calibration]] in Reading Assessment
> > The analysis identifies miscalibrated monitoring signals as central to comprehension failure, but the question of how to *measure* and *train* metacognitive calibration in reading specifically is a rich extension. How do researchers assess calibration accuracy — the match between reported comprehension and actual comprehension? What calibration training protocols have been shown to work? This connects directly to the [[Metacognitive-Calibration]] literature and the measurement questions that this analysis brackets.
> 
> > [!topic-idea] [[Self-Explanation-Effect]] as Architecture, Not Elaboration
> > This analysis reframes the self-explanation effect as evidence for the externalization principle rather than the traditional elaboration account. A focused analysis of the self-explanation research from this architectural perspective — specifically asking whether the monitoring-externalization component and the elaboration component can be experimentally dissociated — would both test the analysis's central claim and extend the [[Self-Explanation-Effect]] literature.
> 
> > [!topic-idea] [[Transfer-of-Learning]] from Instructed to Spontaneous Monitoring
> > The analysis identified the lack of transfer from instructed to spontaneous monitoring as the field's central unresolved challenge. A dedicated treatment of this problem — connecting to the [[Transfer-of-Learning]] literature on near vs. far transfer, on fading scaffolds, and on the conditions for spontaneous application of trained strategies — would directly address the limitation identified in Phase V.
> 
> > [!topic-idea] [[Working-Memory-Capacity]] and Individual Differences in Monitoring Vulnerability
> > Phase IV argues that working memory constraints make monitoring most vulnerable precisely when it is most needed. A focused analysis of individual differences in this vulnerability — asking whether readers with higher working memory capacity are less susceptible to the fluency trap and monitoring-regulation decoupling — would both test the mechanistic account and connect to the broader [[Working-Memory-Capacity]] and reading comprehension literature.
> 
> > [!topic-idea] Monitoring-Regulation Decoupling as Transfer Target: The Three-Mechanism Model Applied to Organizational Learning
> > Phase VII identified the structural analogue between reading monitoring failure and project management monitoring failure. A dedicated transfer-oriented analysis — applying the three-mechanism decoupling model (signal threshold, strategy activation, effort abandonment) systematically to organizational monitoring systems — would extend the principles identified here into the organizational learning and systems design literature. This is the primary transfer-oriented expansion topic for this analysis.
> 
> > [!topic-idea] [[Pseudometacognition]] and the "Performing Monitoring" Problem
> > The analysis focuses on genuine monitoring failure, but a related and underexplored problem is *performative* monitoring — readers who produce the outputs of monitoring (annotations, question lists) without the underlying cognitive process. [[Pseudometacognition]] in the reading context deserves a focused analysis that distinguishes superficial strategy compliance from genuine monitoring engagement, and that examines the conditions under which externalization protocols devolve into performative rather than functional monitoring.
> 
> > [!topic-idea] [[Situation-Model]] Construction and Breakdown: A Deeper Dive
> > This analysis treats the situation model as the target of Tier 3 monitoring without fully examining *how* situation models are constructed and how their construction fails. A focused analysis of situation model breakdown — when readers construct incomplete, incoherent, or subtly incorrect situation models — and its relationship to the monitoring signals it generates would provide the architectural depth that Tier 3 monitoring requires for precise intervention design.

> [!further-exploration] From: [[reading-fluency-automaticity-focused-analysis-2026-03-20|reading-fluency-automaticity-focused-analysis-2026-03-20]]
> **Deepening Your Practice**
> 
> > [!topic-idea] **[[Phonological-Awareness-and-Fluency-Development]]** *(new PKB node)*
> > The phonological awareness research tradition — distinguishing phonological sensitivity, phonological memory, and phonological recoding in lexical access — provides the developmental precursors to the automaticity mechanisms analyzed here. A focused note would examine how phonological awareness instruction in pre-literacy and early literacy builds the phonological representation quality that determines the speed and accuracy with which grapheme-phoneme correspondences can be automatized through reading practice. Connects to [[Phonological-Loop]] and [[Schema-Automation]].
> 
> > [!topic-idea] **[[Deliberate-Practice-and-the-Competence-Need-—-When-Effortful-Learning-is-Motivat|Deliberate Practice and Fluency Development]]**
> > The relationship between deliberate practice theory (Ericsson) and fluency-building practice in reading is conceptually rich. Deliberate practice requires operating at the edge of current competence — but fluency-building practice requires operating within comfortable competence (95-98% accuracy text) to maximize practice-volume-per-unit-time. These prescriptions conflict. A focused analysis would examine whether fluency development is best understood as deliberate practice or as high-volume proceduralization, and what the difference implies for instructional design.
> 
> > [!topic-idea] **[[Fluency-Assessment-and-the-Accuracy-Automaticity-Gap]]** *(new PKB node)*
> > The compensation trap identified in this analysis — accurate-but-slow readers who are invisible to error-rate assessment — suggests a significant gap in current reading assessment practice. A focused analysis of fluency assessment methodology would examine the evidence for different assessment formats (WCPM, prosody rubrics, silent reading rate, maze tasks) and their differential ability to detect automaticity bottlenecks in readers who have compensated through rate reduction. Connects to [[Metacognitive-Monitoring]] and [[Formative-Assessment]].
> 
> > [!topic-idea] **[[Automaticity-and-Skill-Hierarchies-in-Athletic-Performance]]** *(transfer-oriented)*
> > A transfer-oriented investigation extending the cognitive bandwidth liberation principle to athletic skill acquisition. Motor learning research on automaticity — the shift from controlled to automatic processing in movement execution — provides a rich parallel to reading fluency research. Key questions: Does motor automaticity liberate attentional bandwidth for tactical and situational awareness in the same way reading automaticity liberates bandwidth for comprehension? What are the practice conditions that most efficiently drive motor automatization? Connects to [[Dreyfus-Skill-Acquisition-Model]], [[Procedural-Memory]], and [[Transfer-of-Learning]].
> 
> > [!topic-idea] **[[Matthew-Effect-Interventions-and-the-Closing-of-Early-Gaps]]** *(new PKB node)*
> > The Matthew Effect in reading is cognitively guaranteed once established — but it is not inevitable from birth. A focused analysis of prevention and early intervention research would examine which instructional approaches successfully interrupt the Matthew Effect trajectory: what timing (kindergarten vs. first grade), what intensity (Tier 2 vs. Tier 3), and what instructional components (phonemic awareness, phonics, fluency volume) are most effective for at-risk early readers. Connects to [[Formative-Assessment]], [[Deliberate-Practice-Log]], and [[Prior-Knowledge-Activation]].
> 
> > [!topic-idea] **[[The-Fluency-Metacognition-Paradox-Instructional-Implications]]** *(new PKB node)*
> > The synthesis in Phase VI identifying that disfluent readers have simultaneously impaired comprehension and impaired comprehension monitoring deserves its own focused analysis. The instructional implications are non-trivial: metacognitive comprehension strategy instruction may be premature (or actively counterproductive) for readers below a fluency threshold because the cognitive bandwidth to execute it is not available. A focused analysis would examine the evidence for metacognitive intervention sequencing, the threshold question, and the design of metacognitive instruction scaffolded for high-cognitive-load reading conditions. Connects to [[Metacognitive-Monitoring]], [[Fluency-Illusion]], and [[Cognitive-Load-Theory]].

> [!further-exploration] From: [[silent-reading-fluency-speed-comprehension-focused-analysis-2026-03-21|silent-reading-fluency-speed-comprehension-focused-analysis-2026-03-21]]
> **Deepening Your Practice**
> 
> 

> [!topic-idea] From: [[silent-reading-fluency-speed-comprehension-focused-analysis-2026-03-21|silent-reading-fluency-speed-comprehension-focused-analysis-2026-03-21]]
> **[[Vocabulary-Acquisition-for-Reading-Automaticity]]**
> 
> A dedicated investigation of the most efficient protocols for building vocabulary to automaticity — beyond definitional learning, into the consolidated, multi-context representations that actually reduce lexical processing load. Should examine spaced repetition optimization for reading (as distinct from vocabulary testing), morphological pattern learning, and the minimum exposure threshold for automaticity consolidation. Connects directly to [[Spaced-Repetition-Systems]], [[Elaborative-Rehearsal]], and [[Levels-of-Processing]].

> [!topic-idea] From: [[silent-reading-fluency-speed-comprehension-focused-analysis-2026-03-21|silent-reading-fluency-speed-comprehension-focused-analysis-2026-03-21]]
> **[[Comprehension-Monitoring-Training-Protocols]]**
> 
> The [[Metacognitive-Monitoring]] analysis in this report identifies comprehension monitoring as both the most important and most vulnerable cognitive process in reading under speed pressure. A dedicated investigation should examine structured self-testing protocols, the optimal frequency and type of comprehension checks during reading, and the evidence base for monitoring training as a transferable skill. Connects to [[Metacognitive-Regulation]], [[Self-Regulated-Learning]], and [[Formative-Assessment]].

> [!topic-idea] From: [[silent-reading-fluency-speed-comprehension-focused-analysis-2026-03-21|silent-reading-fluency-speed-comprehension-focused-analysis-2026-03-21]]
> **[[Domain-Expertise-and-Reading-Speed-A-Transfer-Investigation]]**
> 
> This expansion topic follows the far-transfer direction: applies the Bottleneck Liberation principle to the question of how expertise development in a target domain should be optimized to accelerate reading speed in that domain. Should examine the relationship between vocabulary automaticity and conceptual schema depth as independent and interactive contributors to reading efficiency. A transfer-oriented investigation testing whether the bottleneck structure identified in reading science maps onto expertise acquisition in other cognitively demanding domains (chess, medical diagnosis, code review).

> [!topic-idea] From: [[silent-reading-fluency-speed-comprehension-focused-analysis-2026-03-21|silent-reading-fluency-speed-comprehension-focused-analysis-2026-03-21]]
> **[[The-Situation-Model-in-Knowledge-Management]]**
> 
> The [[Situation-Model|situation model]] is the gold standard for reading comprehension, but it has underexplored implications for knowledge management design. Notes that support situation model construction — providing the inferential bridges that sparse propositions leave implicit, encoding causal and temporal relationships explicitly, connecting propositions to broader schemas — are more comprehension-supporting than those that merely record propositions. A design-oriented investigation of how PKB note-making practices can be optimized for situation model construction rather than mere propositional capture.

> [!topic-idea] From: [[silent-reading-fluency-speed-comprehension-focused-analysis-2026-03-21|silent-reading-fluency-speed-comprehension-focused-analysis-2026-03-21]]
> **[[AI-Assisted-Reading-Comprehension-Risks-and-Safeguards]]**
> 
> An applied investigation of the monitoring displacement risk when AI summarization tools accelerate information intake. The structural parallel with speed-reading — fast, fluent processing that may bypass genuine situation model construction — is analytically well-grounded, but the specific magnitude of the comprehension risk and the most effective safeguards require dedicated investigation. Should examine protocols for calibrating AI-assisted reading against comprehension of primary sources.

> [!further-exploration] From: [[schema-construction-problem-focused-analysis-2026-03-22|schema-construction-problem-focused-analysis-2026-03-22]]
> **Deepening Your Practice**
> 
> > [!topic-idea] [[Schema-Automation-and-Fluency-Development]]
> > Examines the post-crystallization phase — how newly constructed schemas become automated through practice, and what this means for the transition from conscious effortful processing to expert fluency. Addresses the relationship between crystallization events and the development of perceptual expertise.
> >
> > **Connection to This Report:** Directly extends Phase IV's post-crystallization analysis.
> > **Priority:** High
> > **Suggested Report Type:** Focused Analysis
> > **Prerequisites:** [[Schema-Crystallization-Event]], [[Schema-Automation]], [[Schema-Theory-and-Learning]]
> 
> > [!topic-idea] [[Analogy-First-Instructional-Design-Practical-Implementation]]
> > A transfer-oriented expansion: develops the Analogy-First Instructional Principle (Phase VI) into a practical design framework for courses, PKB onboarding sequences, and self-directed learning in genuinely novel domains. Would include case studies and design protocols.
> >
> > **Connection to This Report:** Directly applies Phase VI's original synthesis.
> > **Priority:** High
> > **Suggested Report Type:** Focused Analysis
> > **Prerequisites:** [[Schema-Construction]], [[Advance-Organizer]], [[Analogical-Reasoning]]
> 
> > [!topic-idea] [[Conceptual-Change-Theory-and-Schema-Restructuring]]
> > Vosniadou's framework theory approach and Chi's knowledge-in-pieces model offer alternative accounts of how schemas change under anomalous data — extending the accommodation/restructuring account into genuine conceptual change (where existing schemas are not merely modified but replaced). Bridges Schema Theory with science education research.
> >
> > **Connection to This Report:** The conceptual change literature directly addresses the restructuring mechanism that this report identifies as Schema Theory's underspecified core.
> > **Priority:** High
> > **Suggested Report Type:** Comparative Synthesis (Schema Theory vs. Framework Theory)
> > **Prerequisites:** [[Schema-Accommodation]], [[Schema-Construction]], [[Schema-Theory-and-Learning]]
> 
> > [!topic-idea] [[PKB-Design-for-Pre-Crystallization-Knowledge-States]]
> > A transfer-oriented investigation: applies the schema construction analysis directly to PKB architecture for genuinely novel domains. What note structures, linking strategies, and capture protocols best support the elemental → associative → schematic progression? Extends [[The-Schema-Progressive-Architecture-for-PKB-Design]].
> >
> > **Connection to This Report:** Directly applies Phase V's PKB implications and Phase VII's application bridge.
> > **Priority:** Critical
> > **Suggested Report Type:** Focused Analysis
> > **Prerequisites:** [[The-Schema-Progressive-Architecture-for-PKB-Design]], [[Schema-Crystallization-Event]], [[Schema-Progressive-Architecture]]

> [!further-exploration] From: [[habit-formation-focused-analysis-2026-03-28|habit-formation-focused-analysis-2026-03-28]]
> **Deepening Your Practice**
> 
> > [!topic-idea] [[Habit-Breaking-—-The-Inhibition-Architecture]]
> > The analysis focused on habit formation; this expansion would address habit breaking from the same mechanistic framework. The key question: since established habits persist despite changed goals (devaluation paradigm), what interventions actually work? Evidence from Wood's contextual disruption strategies, Acceptance and Commitment Therapy's defusion techniques, and Implementation Intentions research on "if-then" planning. The deeper question concerns whether competing habit formation is structurally necessary for durable habit breaking.
> >
> > **Connection to This Report:** Direct extension of the devaluation asymmetry and the parallel systems problem identified in Phase III and IV.
> > **Priority:** High
> > **Suggested Report Type:** Focused Analysis
> > **Prerequisites:** [[Habit-Formation]], [[Behavioral-Modification]], [[Cognitive-Behavioral-Therapy]]
> 
> > [!topic-idea] [[Implementation Intentions and the if-then Architecture]]
> > Peter Gollwitzer's implementation intentions research demonstrates that "if-then" planning (If I am in situation X, I will perform behavior Y) dramatically improves behavioral follow-through compared to simple goal intentions alone. This is mechanistically interesting in light of the habit formation analysis: implementation intentions may function as artificial context-action bindings — deliberate specifications of the contextual configuration that, with sufficient practice, may accelerate the transition to genuine automaticity. A focused analysis would examine whether implementation intentions are a formation accelerant or a compensatory strategy that maintains goal-directed control.
> >
> > **Connection to This Report:** Direct application of the context-action encoding mechanism to a well-researched behavioral intervention.
> > **Priority:** High
> > **Suggested Report Type:** Focused Analysis
> > **Prerequisites:** [[Habit-Formation]], [[Self-Regulation]], [[Goal-Orientation]]
> 
> > [!topic-idea] [[Automaticity Across Domains — Transfer Investigation]]
> > A transfer-oriented investigation: applying the context-stability and scaffolding-withdrawal principles from this habit formation analysis to reading fluency development, deliberate practice in skill acquisition, and PKB workflow design. This would ground Phase VII's structural analogues in domain-specific evidence, testing whether the prediction — that context stability is the operative variable across these domains — holds empirically.
> >
> > **Connection to This Report:** Direct expansion of Phase VII's FAR transfer section; operationalizes the abstract transfer principles as empirically testable domain-specific predictions.
> > **Priority:** High
> > **Suggested Report Type:** Comparative Synthesis
> > **Prerequisites:** [[Automaticity]], [[Reading-Fluency]], [[Deliberate-Practice]], [[Skill-Acquisition]]
> 
> > [!topic-idea] [[The Metacognition-Automaticity Interface — A First Principles Investigation]]
> > The unresolved question from Phase V's limitations: can metacognitive monitoring of a behavior accelerate or does it delay the automaticity transition? This investigation would examine the dual-system architecture from a metacognitive angle, drawing on the Nelson-Narens monitoring-control model, the SRL cycle's monitoring phase, and the [[Pseudometacognition]] research to resolve whether monitoring during vs. between habit executions has differential effects on automaticity development.
> >
> > **Connection to This Report:** Directly addresses the most important open question identified in Phase V.
> > **Priority:** Medium
> > **Suggested Report Type:** First Principles Investigation
> > **Prerequisites:** [[Self-Regulated-Learning]], [[Metacognition]], [[Habit-Formation]], [[Automaticity]]

> > A transfer-oriented investigation: applies the schema construction analysis directly to PKB architecture for genuinely novel domains. What note structures, linking strategies, and capture protocols best support the elemental → associative → schematic progression? Extends [[The-Schema-Progressive-Architecture-for-PKB-Design]].
> >
> > **Connection to This Report:** Directly applies Phase V's PKB implications and Phase VII's application bridge.
> > **Priority:** Critical
> > **Suggested Report Type:** Focused Analysis
> > **Prerequisites:** [[The-Schema-Progressive-Architecture-for-PKB-Design]], [[Schema-Crystallization-Event]], [[Schema-Progressive-Architecture]]

> [!further-exploration] From: [[silent-reading-fluency-speed-comprehension-focused-analysis-2026-03-21|silent-reading-fluency-speed-comprehension-focused-analysis-2026-03-21]]
> **Deepening Your Practice**
> 
> 

> [!topic-idea] From: [[silent-reading-fluency-speed-comprehension-focused-analysis-2026-03-21|silent-reading-fluency-speed-comprehension-focused-analysis-2026-03-21]]
> **[[Vocabulary-Acquisition-for-Reading-Automaticity]]**
> 
> A dedicated investigation of the most efficient protocols for building vocabulary to automaticity — beyond definitional learning, into the consolidated, multi-context representations that actually reduce lexical processing load. Should examine spaced repetition optimization for reading (as distinct from vocabulary testing), morphological pattern learning, and the minimum exposure threshold for automaticity consolidation. Connects directly to [[Spaced-Repetition-Systems]], [[Elaborative-Rehearsal]], and [[Levels-of-Processing]].

> [!topic-idea] From: [[silent-reading-fluency-speed-comprehension-focused-analysis-2026-03-21|silent-reading-fluency-speed-comprehension-focused-analysis-2026-03-21]]
> **[[Comprehension-Monitoring-Training-Protocols]]**
> 
> The [[Metacognitive-Monitoring]] analysis in this report identifies comprehension monitoring as both the most important and most vulnerable cognitive process in reading under speed pressure. A dedicated investigation should examine structured self-testing protocols, the optimal frequency and type of comprehension checks during reading, and the evidence base for monitoring training as a transferable skill. Connects to [[Metacognitive-Regulation]], [[Self-Regulated-Learning]], and [[Formative-Assessment]].

> [!topic-idea] From: [[silent-reading-fluency-speed-comprehension-focused-analysis-2026-03-21|silent-reading-fluency-speed-comprehension-focused-analysis-2026-03-21]]
> **[[Domain-Expertise-and-Reading-Speed-A-Transfer-Investigation]]**
> 
> This expansion topic follows the far-transfer direction: applies the Bottleneck Liberation principle to the question of how expertise development in a target domain should be optimized to accelerate reading speed in that domain. Should examine the relationship between vocabulary automaticity and conceptual schema depth as independent and interactive contributors to reading efficiency. A transfer-oriented investigation testing whether the bottleneck structure identified in reading science maps onto expertise acquisition in other cognitively demanding domains (chess, medical diagnosis, code review).

> [!topic-idea] From: [[silent-reading-fluency-speed-comprehension-focused-analysis-2026-03-21|silent-reading-fluency-speed-comprehension-focused-analysis-2026-03-21]]
> **[[The-Situation-Model-in-Knowledge-Management]]**
> 
> The [[Situation-Model|situation model]] is the gold standard for reading comprehension, but it has underexplored implications for knowledge management design. Notes that support situation model construction — providing the inferential bridges that sparse propositions leave implicit, encoding causal and temporal relationships explicitly, connecting propositions to broader schemas — are more comprehension-supporting than those that merely record propositions. A design-oriented investigation of how PKB note-making practices can be optimized for situation model construction rather than mere propositional capture.

> [!topic-idea] From: [[silent-reading-fluency-speed-comprehension-focused-analysis-2026-03-21|silent-reading-fluency-speed-comprehension-focused-analysis-2026-03-21]]
> **[[AI-Assisted-Reading-Comprehension-Risks-and-Safeguards]]**
> 
> An applied investigation of the monitoring displacement risk when AI summarization tools accelerate information intake. The structural parallel with speed-reading — fast, fluent processing that may bypass genuine situation model construction — is analytically well-grounded, but the specific magnitude of the comprehension risk and the most effective safeguards require dedicated investigation. Should examine protocols for calibrating AI-assisted reading against comprehension of primary sources.

## Cognitive Psychology/Metacognition

> [!further-exploration] From: [[metacognition-in-learning-focused-analysis-2026-03-20|metacognition-in-learning-focused-analysis-2026-03-20]]
> **Deepening Your Practice**
> 
> > [!topic-idea] [[Metacognitive-Accuracy-as-a-Skill-—-Training-Protocols-and-Development-Trajector|Metacognitive Accuracy as a Trainable Skill]]
> > What do structured training protocols for metacognitive accuracy look like, and what is the developmental trajectory? The monitoring infrastructure analysis here identifies *why* accuracy is hard to train (cue invalidity, domain dependency), but the more applied question is what training designs actually shift accuracy reliably. This investigation should interrogate the distinction between training monitoring accuracy versus training cue ecology change — a distinction the current analysis suggests is crucial.
> 
> > [!topic-idea] [[Algorithmic-Metacognition-—-When-Spaced-Repetition-Systems-Do-Metacognitive-Work|Algorithmic Metacognition]]
> > Spaced repetition systems (SRS) and other algorithmic learning tools perform some of the monitoring and regulatory functions that human metacognition handles poorly. The analysis here raises an interesting question: to what extent do external algorithmic systems compensate for the structural fragility of the monitoring-control coupling? And does relying on algorithmic monitoring produce any atrophying of internal metacognitive infrastructure? This is a transfer-oriented investigation: applying the infrastructure model to the design and evaluation of AI-assisted learning tools.
> 
> > [!topic-idea] [[Social-Metacognition-—-When-Other-Minds-Improve-Your-Monitoring|Social Metacognition]]
> > The monitoring-control coupling problem analyzed here is fundamentally individual — but monitoring and regulation can be distributed across social relationships. Peer feedback, Socratic dialogue, and collaborative learning all provide external monitoring inputs that bypass the low-validity cue problem. This investigation should analyze how social structures can serve as coupling infrastructure, potentially compensating for the structural fragility of individual metacognitive monitoring.
> 
> > [!topic-idea] [[Metacognitive-Transfer-—-Does-PKB-Monitoring-Skill-Generalize-Across-Domains|Metacognitive Transfer Across Domains]]
> > The analysis argued that metacognitive skill is domain-specific in important ways. But the FAR transfer phase suggests that the *structural* insights about monitoring-control coupling can transfer. This tension — domain specificity of calibration versus domain generality of structural patterns — is worth explicit investigation. Does training metacognitive infrastructure in one domain produce any transfer of the infrastructure itself to other domains, or only transfer of the abstract understanding of the coupling problem?
> 
> > [!topic-idea] [[Double-Loop-Learning|Double-Loop Learning and Metacognitive Infrastructure in Organizations]]
> > Argyris and Schön's double-loop learning framework describes organizational learning that changes the governing assumptions behind action, not just the actions themselves. This is structurally analogous to the threshold recalibration and repertoire expansion components of the infrastructure model. Investigating this connection would extend the transfer analysis in Phase VII and illuminate the organizational conditions that support or inhibit the monitoring-control coupling at the collective level.
> 
> > [!topic-idea] [[Motivated-Reasoning|Motivated Reasoning as a Metacognitive Coupling Disruptor]]
> > The threshold mechanism identified motivated suppression as one way accurate monitoring signals fail to drive regulatory action. [[Motivated-Reasoning|Motivated reasoning]] research more broadly documents how emotional and motivational investments shape information processing in ways that bypass deliberate monitoring. A dedicated investigation of motivated reasoning as a coupling disruptor — focusing on the specific mechanism by which emotional stakes recalibrate the regulatory threshold — would deepen the threshold sensitivity analysis considerably. This is a transfer-oriented investigation: applying the coupling framework to understanding why accurate assessment of politically or emotionally charged topics so frequently fails to produce attitude change.

## Cognitive Science

> [!further-exploration] From: [[mental-models-johnson-laird-first-principles-report-2026-03-11|mental-models-johnson-laird-first-principles-report-2026-03-11]]
> **Expansion Topics**
> 
> > [!topic-idea]
> > **Topic**: Oaksford & Chater's Probabilistic Mental Models
> > **Report Type**: First Principles
> > **Description**: A first-principles inquiry into whether the probabilistic rational analysis framework constitutes a genuinely distinct theory of reasoning or is better understood as a formal implementation of the axioms identified in this report. The investigation would audit the assumption that Bayesian inference is the appropriate normative standard for everyday reasoning and derive what the probabilistic account requires vs. assumes.
> > **Core Concepts**: Rational analysis methodology, prior probabilities in reasoning, Bayesian inference as normativity, the probability heuristics model
> > **Related Topics**: Reasoning norms and naturalism, philosophy of normativity, ecological rationality
> 
> > [!topic-idea]
> > **Topic**: The Format of Mental Representation — Empirical and Philosophical Boundaries
> > **Report Type**: Foundational
> > **Description**: A comprehensive landscape map of the analogical-vs-propositional representation debate: its history from the imagery debates of the 1970s through embodied cognition and predictive processing accounts. Would survey the neuroimaging evidence, computational modeling approaches, and philosophical arguments for and against the format distinction that Assumption 1 in this report found insufficiently established.
> > **Core Concepts**: Dual coding theory, perceptual symbol systems (Barsalou), format underdetermination, Pylyshyn's tacit knowledge objection, predictive coding
> > **Related Topics**: Cognitive neuroscience of representation, embodied cognition, philosophy of mind
> 
> > [!topic-idea]
> > **Topic**: The Pragmatic Calibration of Everyday Reasoning
> > **Report Type**: First Principles
> > **Description**: A first-principles inquiry into the "pragmatic construction" insight derived in Phase IV — the hypothesis that what looks like deductive failure is often adaptive probabilistic calibration. Would audit the assumption that laboratory deductive tasks measure the same cognitive processes as everyday reasoning, derive what an adequate account of everyday reasoning must explain, and reconstruct from axioms what it means for reasoning to be "good enough."
> > **Core Concepts**: Ecological validity, naturalistic decision making, fast and frugal heuristics (Gigerenzer), bounded rationality, normativity in cognition
> > **Related Topics**: Heuristics and biases tradition, dual process theory, philosophy of rationality
> 
> > [!topic-idea]
> > **Topic**: Dual Process Theory
> > **Report Type**: First Principles
> > **Description**: Following from the dissolution of the rule/model dichotomy in this report, a first-principles inquiry into whether System 1/System 2 is itself a theoretically grounded distinction or another artifact of a particular experimental tradition. Would audit the type-1/type-2 binary, the normative/descriptive conflation in dual process research, and reconstruct what evidence actually requires.
> > **Core Concepts**: System 1/System 2, autonomous vs. controlled processes, default-interventionist models, parallel competitive models
> > **Related Topics**: Cognitive control, working memory, metacognition
> 
> > [!topic-idea]
> > **Topic**: Reasoning Interventions — What the Evidence Actually Supports
> > **Report Type**: Foundational
> > **Description**: A comprehensive survey of empirically validated interventions for improving reasoning, designed to be read alongside this report. Would inventory training studies, educational interventions, and environmental design approaches, assessing which are format-specific (require assuming mental models or mental logic) and which are format-agnostic (work regardless of the representational debate).
> > **Core Concepts**: Argument mapping, counterexample training, debiasing, informal logic instruction, decision support systems
> > **Related Topics**: Educational psychology, behavioral economics, human factors

> > **Report Type**: First Principles
> > **Description**: A first-principles inquiry into the "pragmatic construction" insight derived in Phase IV — the hypothesis that what looks like deductive failure is often adaptive probabilistic calibration. Would audit the assumption that laboratory deductive tasks measure the same cognitive processes as everyday reasoning, derive what an adequate account of everyday reasoning must explain, and reconstruct from axioms what it means for reasoning to be "good enough."
> > **Core Concepts**: Ecological validity, naturalistic decision making, fast and frugal heuristics (Gigerenzer), bounded rationality, normativity in cognition
> > **Related Topics**: Heuristics and biases tradition, dual process theory, philosophy of rationality
> 
> > [!topic-idea]
> > **Topic**: Dual Process Theory
> > **Report Type**: First Principles
> > **Description**: Following from the dissolution of the rule/model dichotomy in this report, a first-principles inquiry into whether System 1/System 2 is itself a theoretically grounded distinction or another artifact of a particular experimental tradition. Would audit the type-1/type-2 binary, the normative/descriptive conflation in dual process research, and reconstruct what evidence actually requires.
> > **Core Concepts**: System 1/System 2, autonomous vs. controlled processes, default-interventionist models, parallel competitive models
> > **Related Topics**: Cognitive control, working memory, metacognition
> 
> > [!topic-idea]
> > **Topic**: Reasoning Interventions — What the Evidence Actually Supports
> > **Report Type**: Foundational
> > **Description**: A comprehensive survey of empirically validated interventions for improving reasoning, designed to be read alongside this report. Would inventory training studies, educational interventions, and environmental design approaches, assessing which are format-specific (require assuming mental models or mental logic) and which are format-agnostic (work regardless of the representational debate).
> > **Core Concepts**: Argument mapping, counterexample training, debiasing, informal logic instruction, decision support systems
> > **Related Topics**: Educational psychology, behavioral economics, human factors

## Cognitive Science Of Reading

> [!further-exploration] From: [[reading-vocabulary-focused-analysis-2026-03-28|reading-vocabulary-focused-analysis-2026-03-28]]
> **Deepening Your Practice**
> 
> > [!topic-idea] [[Morphological-Knowledge-and-Vocabulary-Acquisition]]
> > A focused analysis of morphological knowledge as the highest-leverage investment for adult vocabulary building. This report would conduct a systematic analysis of the highest-priority root morphemes in English academic and literary vocabulary, mapping the morphological families they generate, and synthesizing the evidence for morphological instruction as a complement to extensive reading. It would address: which morphemes to study first for maximum coverage expansion, how morphological instruction interacts with reading-based acquisition, and what instructional sequences maximize morphological leverage.
> >
> > **Connection to This Report:** Directly follows from Phase IV's morphological leverage analysis and the deliberate practice protocol in Appendix G.
> > **Priority:** Critical
> > **Suggested Report Type:** Focused Analysis
> > **Prerequisites:** [[Morphological-Knowledge]], [[Verbal-Efficiency-Theory]], [[Schema-Theory]]
> 
> > [!topic-idea] [[Spaced-Repetition-Systems-and-Vocabulary-Depth]]
> > An analysis of how spaced repetition systems ([[Spaced-Repetition]], [[Spacing-Effect]]) can be designed specifically to develop deep lexical knowledge — not just recognition-level form-meaning mapping but collocational, morphological, and register knowledge. The report would examine the evidence on card design for depth (cloze cards vs. definition cards vs. production cards), the spacing algorithm implications of building full lexical quality, and how SR practice integrates with extensive reading to create the dual-mode acquisition system identified in Phase V.
> >
> > **Connection to This Report:** The complement hypothesis in Phase V identifies SR as the intentional study mode that fills what reading cannot provide. This report would design the optimal SR practice for vocabulary.
> > **Priority:** High
> > **Suggested Report Type:** Focused Analysis
> > **Prerequisites:** [[Spaced-Repetition-Systems]], [[Spacing-Effect]], [[Elaborative-Rehearsal]], [[Retrieval-Practice]]
> 
> > [!topic-idea] [[The-Simple-View-of-Reading-and-Vocabulary]]
> > A focused analysis of how the Simple View of Reading (Gough & Tunmer, 1986: Reading Comprehension = Decoding × Language Comprehension) positions vocabulary within the reading comprehension architecture. The analysis would examine how vocabulary contributes to the "language comprehension" component, how the SVC model relates to the Verbal Efficiency Theory, and what the model implies for vocabulary instruction at different developmental stages.
> >
> > **Connection to This Report:** The Simple View frames the broader context within which the Cognitive Slack Model operates — this expansion would situate the mechanisms in the larger comprehension architecture.
> > **Priority:** High
> > **Suggested Report Type:** Foundational
> > **Prerequisites:** [[Simple-View-of-Reading]], [[Reading-Fluency]], [[Verbal-Efficiency-Theory]]
> 
> > [!topic-idea] [[Extensive-Reading-Programs-and-Second-Language-Vocabulary]]
> > A comparative analysis examining whether the mechanisms identified in this report (coverage threshold, cognitive slack, depth-frequency multiplier) operate identically in L2 acquisition or require modification. The coverage threshold may be different for L2 readers; the role of L1 morphological knowledge in L2 inference is underspecified; and motivational factors may have different effects. This report would synthesize the L2 extensive reading literature (Nation, Krashen, Day & Bamford) in light of the cognitive mechanism analysis.
> >
> > **Transfer Origin:** The Coverage-Efficiency Threshold principle from Phase VII — this topic investigates whether the principle operates identically in a structurally parallel learning context.
> > **Priority:** Medium
> > **Suggested Report Type:** Comparative Synthesis
> > **Prerequisites:** [[Incidental-Learning]], [[Transfer-of-Learning]], [[Reading-Fluency]]
> 
> > [!topic-idea] [[Print-Exposure-and-General-Knowledge-Accumulation]]
> > An expansion of the Matthew Effect analysis beyond vocabulary to the broader question of how extensive reading shapes general knowledge, analogical reasoning, and cultural literacy. Drawing on Stanovich's print exposure research and the situated cognition literature, this report would examine whether the mechanisms that drive vocabulary acquisition from reading also drive knowledge acquisition more broadly — and what the implications are for reading selection and engagement strategies.
> >
> > **Connection to This Report:** Extends the Matthew Effect analysis from Phase I/IV beyond vocabulary to general cognitive outcomes of extensive reading.
> > **Priority:** Medium
> > **Suggested Report Type:** Focused Analysis
> > **Prerequisites:** [[Stanovich]], [[Schema-Theory]], [[Situated-Learning-Theory]]
> 
> > [!topic-idea] [[Deliberate-Vocabulary-Practice-Design-for-Advanced-Learners]]
> > A practical, protocol-oriented report synthesizing the evidence on deliberate vocabulary practice design for adults who have already reached the 98% coverage threshold for general text. This report would address: what vocabulary levels to target next (academic word lists, domain-specific vocabulary, literary vocabulary), how to integrate intentional study with reading practice for mutual reinforcement, and how to design SR cards for full lexical quality rather than just recognition. This is the direct practical application of the complement hypothesis.
> >
> > **Connection to This Report:** Phase V's conclusion that reading and intentional study are complements with different functions leaves open the question of how to optimally design the intentional study component. This topic fills that gap.
> > **Priority:** Critical
> > **Suggested Report Type:** Focused Analysis
> > **Prerequisites:** [[Spaced-Repetition-Systems]], [[Desirable-Difficulties]], [[Retrieval-Practice]], [[Elaborative-Rehearsal]]
